entities.summary:
The Bank of Italy (Banca d'Italia) is Italy's central bank, founded in 1893 from the merger of three earlier banks of issue. As a member of the European System of Central Banks, the Bank of Italy participates in ECB monetary policy but maintains its supervisory and regulatory functions for Italian banks. Italy's banking tradition is among the world's oldest: the Banca Monte dei Paschi di Siena, founded 1472, is the world's oldest surviving bank.

The Bank of Italy was established during Italy's banking crisis of 1893, when multiple banks of issue had failed due to the real estate speculation collapse of the 1880s-90s. The new unified bank was given the monopoly on issuing Italian lire and gradually took on supervisory functions for the Italian banking system. Governor Donato Menichella (1948-1960) played a crucial role in Italy's post-WWII economic reconstruction, managing the lira stabilization and laying foundations for Italy's 'economic miracle' of the 1950s-60s.

The Bank of Italy's relationship with the ECB has been complex: as one of the ECB's major shareholders (17.5%), Italy has significant influence over euro policy. But ECB rules about monetary financing of government debt have constrained the Bank of Italy's traditional role of supporting Italian government bond markets during fiscal crises, creating tensions during the 2011-2012 Eurozone sovereign debt crisis when Italian 10-year bond yields approached 7%.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Bank of Italy's stewardship of the lira through Italy's economic miracle and its integration into the ECB framework make it central to both Italy's postwar prosperity and the ongoing tensions of European monetary union.
